articles.title: Exercise can sometimes cause chest pain – and this condition may be to blame
articles.author: Helen Rainford, Lead for Primary Care, School of Medicine and Dentistry, University of Lancashire
paras: As a GP, I know that chest pain is one symptom that makes people worry. The immediate concern is that it’s a sign there’s something seriously wrong – such as a problem with their heart or lungs.

But these aren’t the only reasons that chest pain can happen. For many otherwise healthy people, especially those who exercise regularly, the sudden onset of chest pain may actually be caused by a painful, yet generally harmless, condition called costochondritis.

Costochondritis occurs when the tissue connecting the ribs to the breastbone becomes irritated. This causes pain at the front of the chest, usually close to the breastbone. Patients describe the pain as sharp, aching or sore, and it’s often aggravated by stretching, twisting, exercise, coughing or taking a deep breath. The area is frequently tender to touch and pressing on it can cause pain.
Costochondritis is thought to be the cause of approximately 13% of GP visits for chest pain. The condition is diagnosed based on a person’s symptoms and examination.

There’s no specific blood test or scan that can confirm costochondritis. Instead, the diagnosis is usually based on a person’s symptoms and a physical examination. However, tests such as an electrocardiogram (ECG), which records the heart’s electrical activity, or a chest x-ray may sometimes be needed to rule out more serious issues. This is particularly important in people aged over 35 years and those with a history of, or risk factors for, coronary heart disease.
What causes costochondritis?
The exact causes of costochondritis aren’t always clear. It’s often linked to strain affecting the area where the ribs join the breastbone.

For many people, the condition is triggered by repetitive physical activity or overuse of the upper body. Weight training, rowing, heavy lifting or exercises involving repeated pushing and pulling movements can place extra stress on the chest wall.

The risk appears to be greatest when exercise intensity increases too quickly. A sudden jump in training volume, frequency or the weight a person is lifting can overload tissues that haven’t had time to adapt.

Costochondritis can also happen after a minor chest injury – such as a fall or a blow sustained during contact sports. Another common trigger is persistent coughing. This places considerable strain on the chest wall’s muscles and tissues, which is why some people develop costochondritis during or after a heavy cold or chest infection.

Understanding what triggered costochondritis is an important part of recovery. Most cases improve with simple self-care measures. The first step is usually trying to temporarily avoid or reduce the activities that provoked the pain – particularly heavy lifting and repetitive upper-body exercise. You should avoid these activities until the pain settles.

Anti-inflammatory pain medicines, such as paracetamol and ibuprofen, can also help reduce symptoms where suitable. Many people also find that applying a heat pack or warm compress helps ease discomfort.

As symptoms begin to settle, gentle chest, shoulder and upper back stretches can help improve mobility and prevent stiffness. For instance, the thoracic extension exercise, in which a person stretches their back over a low chair while their hands are placed behind their head, showed benefit for some patients.
Costochondritis often improves on its own. Symptoms may last for a several weeks or several months, but most people make a full recovery within a year.
Can costochondritis be prevented?

It’s not always possible to prevent costochondritis, but a few sensible precautions can reduce the risk. If you’re starting a new exercise programme or increasing your weights, build up gradually and give your body time to adapt. Good lifting technique, whether in the gym or at work, can also reduce unnecessary strain on the chest wall.

It’s also important to avoid overtraining. Exercising too hard, too often or without adequate recovery increases the risk of overuse injuries, including costochondritis. Rest days are not a sign of weakness; they are part of training.
Don’t forget stretching. Regular stretching can also help maintain flexibility and mobility in the chest, shoulders and upper back.

Most importantly, don’t ignore pain. If your chest wall starts hurting during exercise, resist the temptation to push through it. Continuing to strain irritated tissues can prolong symptoms and delay recovery.

Costochondritis can be painful and worrying, but it’s usually not a serious condition. Just make sure you don’t dismiss any chest pain you’re experiencing or assume it’s costochondritis. This is especially key if your chest pain is severe, feels tight or heavy, or the pain spreads to the arm, neck, jaw or back. Similarly seek medical advice if the pain is accompanied by other symptoms – such as shortness of breath, nausea, sweating or dizziness.
Once more serious causes have been excluded, most people recover fully with a combination of rest, a gradual return to activity and sensible exercise habits.

articles.title: Leave home with a plan: What to pack in your medical kit and when to seek care for symptoms abroad
articles.author: Andrés Henao, Professor of Medicine and Infectious Disease, University of Colorado Anschutz
paras: When people prepare to see a doctor before an international trip, vaccines usually dominate the conversation.

And while vaccines are important, many of the health problems most likely to derail a trip cannot be prevented with a vaccine: Diarrhea, respiratory infections, motion sickness and flare-ups of existing medical conditions are all common – and none of them can be headed off with a shot.

The U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention estimates that between 43% and 79% of travelers to low- and middle-income countries become ill during or after their trip, although most of those illnesses are mild.
As an infectious diseases physician who specializes in travel and tropical medicine, I counsel many patients before they leave the country and care for them when they come home sick.

A good pretravel visit to the doctor should end with more than a list of shots. You should know which illnesses you could encounter on your itinerary, which symptoms you can reasonably handle yourself, which medicines to carry and how to use them, and which warning signs mean it is time to find a doctor.

Infectious disease risks abroad are constantly shifting. A good healthcare provider who specializes in travel and geographic medicine keeps up with these developments so that the advice you get reflects what is happening now, not last year.
Since early 2025, South America has seen new yellow fever outbreaks that redrew long-standing risk maps and an unusual hantavirus cluster that spread from person to person aboard a cruise ship.

Cases of dengue fever worldwide roughly doubled in a single year, and another tropical disease – chikungunya – also flared in new places, including the largest outbreak ever recorded in China. Fiji declared a fast-growing HIV outbreak. And common respiratory viruses, from influenza to COVID-19, continue to circulate all over the world.

In my own clinical research with colleagues, we have seen travelers who returned to the U.S. with serious – and occasionally fatal – infections, such as malaria and hepatitis, often after dangerous delays in recognizing what was wrong.
Let your itinerary guide the conversation
Travel health advice is not one-size-fits-all. A week at a Caribbean resort, a safari in East Africa and a month trekking in Nepal carry very different risks.

Even the likely cause of a fever changes with the destination. Dengue is a leading concern after travel in much of Latin America and Asia, while malaria is especially important in parts of sub-Saharan Africa, and typhoid and paratyphoid fever loom largest in South Asia.
What you do matters, too – freshwater swimming, visiting caves, animal contact, hiking and staying in remote areas each add their own hazards.

So bring your actual itinerary to the appointment. Tell your doctor not just which countries you’ll visit, but whether you’ll be in cities or the countryside, what you plan to do, how high you’ll go, how long you’ll stay and how easily you could reach a reliable hospital.
Illnesses you can safely treat yourself

For minor illnesses, you can plan to treat yourself. Travelers’ diarrhea is the best example of such an illness. Depending on the destination and season, it affects an estimated 10% to 40% of travelers during the first two weeks of a trip. Most cases clear up on their own within a few days, but having a plan makes a real difference.

Ask your doctor what to do if diarrhea develops. Oral rehydration salts help replace fluids when losses are heavy. Loperamide, an over-the-counter antidiarrheal, can reduce how often and how urgently you need a bathroom, but it should not be used on its own when diarrhea comes with a fever or blood in the stool. Depending on your destination and medical history, your doctor may also give you an antibiotic to carry and use only for moderate or severe diarrhea.

When it comes to treatments you’ll be administering yourself, it’s as important to ask your doctor when to use each medicine as it is to have the drugs on hand. Antibiotics have side effects, can leave you carrying drug-resistant bacteria and contribute to antibiotic resistance worldwide – so they are best saved for the episodes that truly need them.

The same logic applies to other predictable problems. Someone prone to seasickness on a planned boat trip might discuss meclizine or a scopolamine patch. A traveler flying straight into a high-altitude city such as Cusco, Peru, or La Paz, Bolivia, might discuss acetazolamide, a prescription medicine that helps the body acclimatize and roughly halves the risk of altitude sickness during rapid ascents.
Build a small medical kit – not a portable pharmacy

A basic travel health kit keeps a small problem from becoming a big one. The contents depend on the traveler and the trip, but useful items include pain and fever medicine, bandages, antiseptic, oral rehydration salts, loperamide, antihistamine and anything prescribed specifically for the trip.

People with chronic conditions should pack enough of their regular medications for the entire trip, plus extra in case of delays. Keep medicines in their original labeled containers, carry them in your hand luggage rather than checked bags, and consider bringing a copy of your prescriptions written with the drugs’ generic names.

Replacing a medication abroad can be harder than you expect. Drugs may have different names, formulations or availability in other countries, and counterfeit or low-quality medicines remain a real problem in some places. Some medications that are routine in the U.S. are restricted or banned elsewhere. Insulin, injectable drugs, controlled substances and anything that needs refrigeration will require extra planning.
Be skeptical of popular travel remedies

Travel medicine is full of remedies with better reputations than evidence. Ginger is often recommended for motion sickness, but studies have produced mixed results. Acupressure wristbands for motion sickness do not outperform placebos. And despite their popularity, probiotics are not recommended for preventing travelers’ diarrhea, as their efficacy is still unknown.

Coca leaves and coca tea are widely used for altitude symptoms in the Andes, but there is no strong evidence that they prevent altitude illness – and the same is true of garlic, ginkgo and vitamin E. “Natural” does not mean effective, or even harmless, particularly when a supplement interacts with a prescription drug.
Ask about when to seek medical care
Perhaps the most important part of any plan is recognizing when self-care is no longer appropriate.

Seek medical attention for severe dehydration, persistent vomiting, difficulty breathing, confusion, severe abdominal pain or an illness that is rapidly getting worse. Bloody diarrhea or diarrhea with a significant fever calls for medical care rather than simply taking an antidiarrheal and carrying on with your trip.

At high altitudes, shortness of breath while resting, confusion, or difficulty walking a straight line are warning signs. Severe altitude illness is treated by descending and getting medical care – another cup of coca tea is not an adequate substitute.

Fever after travel to an area where malaria is common deserves special attention. Malaria can turn deadly within hours, so get evaluated promptly and make sure the clinician knows where you have been. Some travel-related infections surface weeks or even months after you get home, which is why your travel history stays relevant long after your suitcase is unpacked.

I encourage travelers to make a medical contingency plan. Ask yourself: If my flight home were canceled and I had to stay abroad another week, would I have enough medication? If I developed diarrhea tomorrow, would I know what to take? If I spiked a fever, would I know when and where to seek care?
International travel will never be risk-free. But preparing for the problems most likely to happen can keep a manageable illness from becoming a medical emergency.

articles.title: Where humans build, mosquitoes follow – bringing dengue, West Nile and other diseases with them
articles.author: Kylee Rae Noel, Postdoctoral Research Associate in Entomology, University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign
paras: A mosquito buzzing in your backyard may seem like a minor annoyance. But these tiny insects, with their taste for human blood, are increasingly appearing in areas where they were once rare or absent, and that’s raising concerns about the spread of mosquito-borne diseases, including West Nile, Zika and dengue fever.
Florida’s struggles with dengue fever in 2026 should be a warning.

Hillsborough County, home to Tampa, had seen more than 350 dengue cases, at least one of them fatal, by late October. Miami-Dade County had reported more than 200 cases, and the statewide number was still rising in what has been described as the largest dengue outbreak in modern Florida history. More than 400 of the over 700 Florida cases, including many of those in Hillsborough County and at least seven in the Orlando area, were listed as locally acquired from mosquitoes in the area.

Climate change is part of the reason people in many parts of the country are seeing more mosquitoes. Rising global temperatures and shorter winters expand the area suitable for mosquitoes to live in and transmit viruses that cause diseases. Climate change also brings increasingly erratic storm systems, heat and rainfall patterns that leave standing water, creating conditions ideal for mosquitoes to breed.
The other major factor shaping where mosquitoes live, often overlooked, is humans themselves.

We study entomology and medical geography, including the spread of mosquito-borne diseases. To understand why you may be seeing more mosquitoes, and why communities like Hillsborough County are spending millions of dollars on attempts to control them, start by looking close to home.
Mosquitoes follow when humans move in

Mosquitoes such as Aedes aegypti – the primary transmitter of pathogens that cause dengue fever, yellow fever, Chikungunya and Zika in the Americas – likely arrived in the U.S. with the slave trade. Both Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus, a transmitter of many of the same diseases but a more recent arrival in the U.S., are moved by the global shipping network, which can take them to new locations and reintroduce them in parts of their ranges where they may have been controlled in the past.
Aedes aegypti’s habits, including its ability to use household environments for living and breeding, have made it a very successful and established invader where climate conditions permit.

A flowerpot saucer, clogged gutter, discarded tire, birdbath or even a bottle cap can collect enough water for mosquito larvae to develop. A single Aedes aegypti mosquito can lay more than 100 eggs at a time up to five times during its lifespan, which is only about a month.
As suburban neighborhoods expand, so do opportunities for mosquitoes to breed and find humans for their meals.
Across the United States, new housing developments create thousands of these small water-holding containers and bring together the two things these mosquitoes need: standing water and people.

This combination allows them to spread through transportation networks, establishing populations far from their original ranges, and explains why mosquito expansion is often linked to patterns of human movement and development.

Aedes albopictus, originally native to Southeast Asia and now found in all habitable continents, provides a striking example of this spread. These mosquitoes arrived in the U.S. mostly because of human actions. They stowed away on boats and other vehicles, often riding in used tires or lucky bamboo.

Their early dispersal in the U.S. has been linked to the interstate highway system. By 2017, Aedes albopictus was documented in 1,368 counties across 40 states, and it has continued to expand across much of the eastern and central U.S.
One of Iowa’s first established Aedes albopictus populations, for example, appeared in the Des Moines metropolitan area, where it has continued to grow and expand to other communities.
Its spread from southeast Asia all the way to the U.S. Midwest demonstrates how globalization and suburban growth can create opportunities for mosquitoes.
US’s most common mosquito threat: West Nile

West Nile virus remains the most widespread mosquito-borne disease in the continental United States. It is primarily transmitted by Culex mosquitoes, including common house mosquitoes, which are found in much of the country.

Culex mosquitoes can breed in a wide range of habitats, including storm drains, roadside ditches, retention ponds, wetlands and other standing water. Their ability to thrive in both urban and rural environments has helped make West Nile virus an enduring public health concern in many states.

Because Culex mosquitoes are already established across much of the country, climate change may not necessarily introduce them to new regions. Instead, research is increasingly focused on how changing temperatures and precipitation patterns could influence their abundance, seasonal activity and ability to transmit disease.
Researchers found that New York state’s season with temperatures suitable for mosquitoes to transmit West Nile virus lengthened by an average of 20 days between 1999 and 2024.

A study conducted by one of us, Sadie Ryan, showed that in Florida, all 67 counties had a suitable season for mosquitoes spreading West Nile virus for five or more months in 2000, and 2.33 million people in Florida experienced a nine-month-long season. By the 2030s, as temperatures warm, the study projects that around 70% of Florida’s population is likely to have a chance of getting West Nile nine months out of the year.

In 2025, for example, Florida took longer to cool down in the fall than usual, leaving moderate temperatures and enough standing water that Aedes mosquitoes could remain active late into the year. Florida saw a rise in dengue cases.
Longer warm seasons means mosquitoes will become a growing public health issue, and controlling them will become increasingly crucial.

articles.title: Migraine remedies are everywhere on social media, but the evidence needs a closer look
articles.author: Amanda Ellison, Professor of Neuroscience, Durham University
paras: When you have a migraine, anything that might ease the pain can become very appealing. On social media, that might mean ordering chips and a Coke or pressing a cold spoon against your forehead. As someone who experiences migraine, I understand the willingness to try something that promises relief.

As a neuroscientist and author of Splitting, a book about headaches including migraine, I want to know what supports that promise. An explanation that sounds plausible needs testing before it becomes reliable treatment advice.
Understanding what happens during an attack helps explain why some remedies might offer comfort, while others promise more than the evidence can support.

Migraine can affect how you feel and function long before your head starts hurting. For me, repeated yawning is a warning sign. Researchers have documented symptoms before the headache, including tiredness and difficulty concentrating. This early phase, called the “prodrome”, can begin hours or even days beforehand.
Food cravings can also occur. That creates a problem when trying to identify triggers: something you eat because an attack has already begun may subsequently get blamed for causing it.

Chocolate is a good example. A review of research found insufficient evidence to recommend that everyone with migraine avoid it. The authors noted that eating chocolate before a headache might reflect a craving during the early phase of an attack, rather than chocolate triggering it. Of course, that does not establish chocolate as a treatment, either.

Some people also experience aura: temporary changes in vision or other sensations. Around a third of people with migraine experience it. Visual symptoms can include flashing lights or missing patches in the visual field.

I once experienced a striking visual disturbance while visiting Saltburn beach. Part of my visual field disappeared, and I expected a headache to follow. It never arrived, and it never does for some people who experience these ocular migraines.

Aura is associated with a slowly spreading wave of altered electrical activity across the brain’s outer surface. Depending on the area affected, people may experience flashing lights, tingling or other symptoms. Migraine aura can occur without a headache, although unfamiliar visual disturbances should be medically assessed because they can have other causes.

When headache develops, it can be accompanied by nausea and sensitivity to light and sound. Untreated or unsuccessfully treated attacks typically last four to 72 hours. Symptoms vary, so being able to carry on with some activities does not rule out migraine.

The end of the pain may not mean the end of the attack. During the recovery phase, called the “postdrome”, people can feel exhausted or struggle to concentrate. An electronic diary study documented these lingering symptoms. The comparison with a hangover is understandable, although there has been no night out to account for it.

This complexity is one reason to be cautious about simple explanations for headache hacks. Migraine has sometimes been explained as a problem of blood vessels widening. But it also involves networks that process pain and sensory information, including signalling between nerves and blood vessels around the brain.

Consider the chips-and-Coke suggestion. Caffeine has a legitimate place in some headache medicines. A Cochrane review, which systematically assessed results from clinical studies, found that adding caffeine to common painkillers modestly improved pain relief across several conditions, including headache.

Caffeine affects chemical signalling in the nervous system as well as blood vessels, but its pain-relieving effects are more complicated than simply narrowing widened vessels. And studies of caffeine added to medicines cannot establish that a fast-food meal treats migraine, or that its salt and sugar “rebalance” the brain.

Caffeine also complicates the picture because suddenly stopping regular consumption can trigger headache. A small randomised trial involving ten people with migraine who regularly consumed substantial amounts of caffeine found that abrupt withdrawal triggered migraine attacks in several participants.

Cooling treatments have some supporting research. A systematic review found evidence of short-term pain relief from cooling interventions, although the six studies used different methods and the certainty of evidence varied. That offers some support for cooling as a comfort measure; it does not establish that holding a cold spoon against your forehead will relieve migraine.

Established treatments deserve attention, too. Triptans, such as sumatriptan, are medicines designed to treat migraine attacks. They act on receptors for serotonin, a chemical messenger involved in nerve signalling, and generally work best when taken early in the headache phase, while pain is still mild.
If attacks are frequent or disabling, discuss preventive treatment with a clinician. Options include medicines targeting CGRP, a chemical messenger involved in migraine.

Between attacks, a headache diary can help you and your clinician understand the pattern. Record symptoms and medication use, alongside possible influences such as changes in sleep and diet. Look for repeated associations before deciding that a particular food must go.
A sudden, extremely painful headache, new weakness, difficulty speaking or sudden loss of vision needs emergency assessment. Do not assume an unfamiliar symptom is migraine.

Understanding your own migraine patterns can help you recognise early warning signs and make informed decisions about care. It will not make every attack preventable, but it may help you act sooner when symptoms begin.

articles.title: Can your brain make you see ghosts? The science behind the Bloody Mary legend
articles.author: Michelle Spear, Professor of Anatomy, University of Bristol
paras: It’s Halloween night. Someone has dared you to turn off the lights and stand in front of the mirror. The rules are simple, stare into your reflection and say her name three times.
Bloody Mary. Bloody Mary. Bloody Mary.

According to the creepy urban legend, a terrifying figure will appear in the glass. Depending on which version of the story you follow, she might be a bloodied woman, a witch or a ghost seeking revenge. Sometimes, she simply appears behind you. In more sinister versions, she reaches out of the mirror.
Most of us encountered some variation of this story as children. Those brave enough to have tried it may even swear they saw a monstrous face appear in the mirror before them.

As tempting as it might be to believe that the monster you saw in mirror was something supernatural, the real explanation is perhaps even stranger. Your brain is perfectly capable of turning your own reflection into something you barely recognise.

In 2010, Italian psychologist Giovanni Caputo published a study with the intriguing title Strange-face-in-the-mirror illusion. He asked 66 volunteers to sit approximately 40 centimetres from a mirror in a dimly lit room and look at their own faces for one minute.

Around two-thirds reported significant distortions of their faces. More than a quarter described seeing an unfamiliar person, while others reported fantastical beings, animals or the faces of relatives – sometimes deceased. Some changes began after less than a minute.
The participants weren’t being asked to summon ghosts. They were simply looking at themselves. So why would something as familiar as our own face suddenly become strange?

The explanation partly lies in the 1804 work done by Swiss physician Ignaz Paul Vital Troxler who described a curious phenomenon. When we fix our gaze on one point, objects elsewhere in our visual field can gradually fade from awareness. This is now known as the Troxler effect, or Troxler fading.

This effect happens partly because sensory neurons, which detect and transmit information about what we see, adapt to relatively constant stimulation. Our visual system is particularly interested in change: movement, shifting contrast and anything that might require our attention.

Normally, we hardly notice this process. Even when we believe we’re staring steadily, our eyes make tiny movements that continually refresh visual information. But prolonged fixation can allow relatively stable features, particularly those away from the centre of our gaze, to become less distinct.

Now imagine applying this to your face. When you stare at your own eyes in a mirror, the surrounding features remain relatively stationary. The contours of your cheeks, the edges of your nose and the outline of your mouth provide a fairly constant pattern of information.

But in dim light, those features are already harder to distinguish – so the Troxler effect alone cannot explain why someone might see an entirely different face. For that, we need to consider how the brain recognises faces.
Human beings are extraordinarily sensitive to faces. We can recognise familiar people from surprisingly little visual information and detect subtle changes in expression.

This ability involves a network of brain regions, including the fusiform face area, which responds particularly strongly to faces. Rather than analysing every feature independently, our visual system processes the relationships between them – including the distance between the eyes, the position of the nose and the arrangement of facial features.

When you look into a mirror, your brain isn’t simply recording what is in front of you. It interprets visual information using previous experience and expectations – and there’s perhaps no face you know better than your own. But under dim lighting, the information arriving from your eyes becomes less reliable. Shadows obscure features, contrast diminishes and the relationships between parts of the face become harder to resolve.
The brain must continue interpreting this increasingly ambiguous information. Sometimes the result is a distorted version of your own face. Sometimes it resembles another person altogether.

The mechanisms behind these illusions are still under investigation. But what makes the experience disturbing is that the reflection remains recognisably human while no longer appearing to belong to you.
Long before children began summoning Bloody Mary, reflective surfaces were associated with spirits, prophecy and the dead.

The ancient practice of catoptromancy involved divination using mirrors. Related traditions of scrying involved gazing into reflective surfaces in the hope of seeing visions or messages hidden from ordinary sight.

Mirrors also acquired significance in mourning traditions. In some communities, they were covered following a death because of the belief they could trap the soul or reveal the dead. Other traditions have different explanations for covering mirrors – including setting aside concerns about personal appearance during mourning.

We cannot conclude that visual illusions gave rise to these customs. But it’s intriguing that prolonged staring, low illumination and the expectation of seeing something unusual feature in both supernatural mirror rituals and experiments producing perceptual distortions.
The Bloody Mary ritual adds another ingredient: anticipation. You expect something frightening, and that expectation may influence how you interpret ambiguous shadows and unfamiliar features.

In this way, the ritual creates the very conditions in which something unsettling might appear. The legend tells you what to expect, and your visual system may provide something that seems to confirm it. So, this Halloween, remember that you don’t need to believe in ghosts for something strange to happen.

articles.title: Protein can help build and preserve muscle, but eating more has its limits
articles.author: Dominic Farsi, Marie Skłodowska-Curie Actions (MSCA) Research Fellow, Teagasc; King's College London; Queen's University Belfast
paras: High protein content has become a selling point on foods ranging from breakfast cereals to yoghurts. For anyone hoping to build muscle or stay strong as they age, choosing the product with the most protein can seem sensible. But whether an extra serving will help depends on what they already eat and how they use their muscles.

Someone who regularly lifts weights may benefit from additional protein to support muscle growth. An older person with a small appetite may need help getting enough to maintain strength. Someone already eating enough protein may gain little from adding more.
Understanding those differences can make it easier to decide whether to change your diet, buy a supplement or concentrate on exercise.
Muscle tissue is continually being broken down and rebuilt. Dietary protein supplies amino acids, the small molecules the body uses to make its own proteins, including those in muscle.

Resistance exercise makes muscles work against a load. That load might come from weights or from your own body during an exercise such as press-ups. It stimulates the processes involved in building and repairing muscle, allowing muscles to adapt to repeated demands.
Protein supports this adaptation, but increasing intake does not reproduce the effects of exercise.

A review of 49 trials involving 1,863 participants found that protein supplements produced additional improvements in muscle size and strength during resistance training. Participants were training for at least six weeks. The findings therefore concern protein’s contribution to a training programme, rather than the effects of adding a shake to an otherwise unchanged routine.
For someone already eating enough protein, establishing a manageable strength-training routine may be more useful than searching for another high-protein snack.
More protein does not mean unlimited gains

The UK reference intake for adults is 0.75g of protein per kilogram of body weight each day. For someone weighing 70kg, that is about 53g. This reference intake is intended to cover the needs of most healthy adults, rather than specifically maximise muscle growth.

People undertaking resistance training may benefit from more. In the review of 49 trials, additional protein did not appear to produce further gains in fat-free mass, which includes muscle, once total daily intake reached around 1.6g per kilogram of body weight. For a 70kg adult, that would be about 112g from all food and supplements combined.

That figure is an estimate across studies, rather than a precise threshold for every person. It does not mean everyone needs to aim for it. Existing protein intake and training demands affect whether additional protein is likely to help.

Before buying supplements, consider the protein already supplied by ordinary meals. A supplement may be convenient when food alone does not meet someone’s protein needs. But if their diet already provides enough protein for their activity level, a supplement may offer little extra benefit while increasing costs.
Maintaining muscle with age
Muscle health has consequences well beyond appearance. Losing strength can make getting out of a chair or carrying shopping harder, threatening independence.

Older muscles can become less responsive to the muscle-building effects of a meal, a phenomenon called “anabolic resistance”. This means the same amount of protein may produce a weaker muscle-building response than it does in younger people.

An international expert group recommends around 1.0–1.2g of protein per kilogram daily for healthy adults over 65, alongside exercise. For someone weighing 70kg, that is about 70–84g. Needs can differ during illness, and people with significant kidney disease may require individual advice.

However, preserving muscle involves more than increasing protein. A year-long trial involving 208 healthy older adults found that protein supplementation alone did not improve muscle size or strength compared with carbohydrate supplementation. Heavy resistance training combined with whey protein produced benefits that supplementation alone did not.

The practical implication is that advice about protein should also consider opportunities to exercise. Increasing intake without addressing inactivity may leave an important part of muscle maintenance neglected.
Choosing foods that fit your diet

Cottage cheese is one convenient source of protein, but plenty of alternatives are available. Other dairy foods and eggs provide protein, as do beans and soy foods. Preferences and affordability will influence which options someone can eat regularly.

Plant-based diets can also support muscle growth. In a small study of 38 young men, vegans and omnivores followed a 12-week resistance-training programme while consuming similar amounts of protein, approximately 1.6g per kilogram daily. Both groups used supplements to reach that intake. Researchers found similar improvements in muscle mass and strength.

The study was small and involved young men, so it cannot establish that every protein source works equally well in every situation. It does show that muscle gains are possible with an exclusively plant-based diet when protein intake and training are adequate.

For general health, the NHS recommends muscle-strengthening activities on at least two days a week. Exercises should suit someone’s abilities and become progressively more difficult as strength improves.

Someone eating too little protein may benefit from changing their meals. Someone already meeting their needs may make more progress by finding a strength-training routine they can sustain. Those decisions depend on the person’s circumstances, which a protein count on a packet cannot capture.

Whether the goal is lifting a heavier weight or getting up the stairs more easily, the useful question is how eating and activity can support that goal together. Buying more protein is only helpful when it addresses something the person actually needs.

articles.title: Fries, cold spoons and eyebrow clamps: investigating the internet’s migraine remedies
articles.author: Katie Edwards, Commissioning Editor, Health + Medicine and Host of Strange Health podcast, The Conversation
paras: If you’ve ever had a migraine, you’ll understand the appeal of anything that promises to make it stop. Even when that advice involves attaching hair clips to your eyebrows.

Social media has plenty of suggestions. Some people swear by a large Coke and McDonald’s fries, which has gained the nickname of a “McMigraine”. Others recommend putting your feet in hot water while cooling the back of your head with spoons. Suddenly, managing a migraine seems to require the logistical planning of a spa day, with a takeaway delivery slot.
But how much science is there behind these remedies? And why can migraine make you feel so dreadful long before your head starts hurting?

In this episode of the Strange Health podcast, I explore the world of migraine and the online hacks promising relief with my co-host Dan Baumgardt, a practising GP and lecturer at the University of Bristol.

Our guest is Amanda Ellison, professor of neuroscience at Durham University and author of Splitting: The Inside Story on Headaches. Amanda experiences migraines herself, so she understands both the biology and the willingness to try something that might help.
When the headache is only part of the story

Migraine can involve nausea and a heightened sensitivity to light or sound. Its effects can also begin hours or even days before the headache, with early symptoms including tiredness and food cravings. Not everyone experiences every stage, and some people have an aura, such as flashing lights or zigzag patterns, without a headache at all.

For Ellison, repeated yawning can be a warning that an attack is approaching. She explains what she notices as her symptoms develop, and describes the peculiar experience of having part of her vision disappear during a trip to the beach.

Then there’s the aftermath. The pain may have subsided, but exhaustion and difficulty concentrating can linger during the recovery phase, sometimes called the “migraine hangover”. There hasn’t even been a night out to account for it.
Chips, Coke and the case against chocolate

Ellison also helps us examine the reasoning behind some popular headache hacks. The important distinction is between a possible explanation for why something might offer comfort and evidence that it reliably treats migraine. Caffeine, for example, can help some people, but excessive consumption or withdrawal can also contribute to attacks. A takeaway order is hardly a carefully controlled treatment.

And in a discussion on migraine triggers, Ellison says chocolate gets a bad rap. If you eat it shortly before a migraine, it’s understandable to suspect a connection. But craving chocolate can itself be an early symptom of an attack that has already begun. The timing can make the snack look guilty.
Along the way, Ellison explains why identifying the kind of headache you have is a useful starting point: something that helps with brain freeze won’t necessarily help with migraine.
Listen to the episode for a lively exploration of what happens during an attack, and why understanding your own symptoms can help you make sense of the advice.

articles.title: If Philadelphia Eagles quarterback Jalen Hurts can get dangerous blood clots, so can you – here’s how some states are trying to reduce the risk
articles.author: Ali Ataya, Professor of Medicine, University of Florida
paras: Jalen Hurts is 28, a Super Bowl MVP and an elite athlete in peak physical condition. He was also recently diagnosed with blood clots in his leg and both lungs.

After a cleat to the left calf during a game against the Los Angeles Rams on Oct. 4, 2026, and after a team flight to London, the Philadelphia Eagles quarterback was given an ultrasound and diagnosed with a superficial vein thrombosis, which is a blood clot in the vein near the skin, in his left leg.
He played that Sunday. A follow-up ultrasound showed the superficial vein clot had progressed to a deeper vein, and he was diagnosed with a deep vein thrombosis, or DVT.

By Oct. 19, he was diagnosed with a bilateral pulmonary embolism, which means he had blood clots in both lungs. He started treatment with blood thinners, and his prognosis was described as “very good,” according to a statement from the team and his agent, but he will likely be out for the rest of the season.

For me, as a pulmonary vascular disease specialist who treats patients with blood clots and pulmonary embolisms, this case highlights an important teaching moment. If this can happen to an elite athlete, it can happen to anyone. And too often, it can be prevented.
Deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism are grouped under one name: venous thromboembolism.

When a deep vein thrombosis develops, the clot can break off and a piece of it can travel through the body and lodge in the arteries in the lungs, where it obstructs blood flow and lowers oxygen in the blood, causing shortness of breath and strain on the heart. This is known as pulmonary embolism. If the blood clot in the lungs is large enough, it can sometimes kill within hours.

Clots that happen near the skin, like the one first found in Hurts’ leg, are often treated as minor but are not always harmless. It is estimated that a quarter of people diagnosed with superficial clots can also have deep vein thrombosis, so health providers order follow-up imaging.

In the United States, up to 900,000 people are affected by venous thromboembolism each year. An estimated 60,000 to 100,000 die from it annually. Survivors often have long-term symptoms such as persistent leg swelling, shortness of breath, chronic clots, or elevated blood pressure in the arteries in the lungs, which is known as chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension.

The three main factors that drive formation of blood clots are injury to the vein wall, slow or stagnant blood flow in that injured region, and blood that clots easily due to inflammation or other factors. This is called Virchow’s triad, and Hurts’ story touches every corner of this triad.

The injury to the left calf bruised the muscle and likely the vein beneath it. Later, prolonged sitting on an overnight flight from Philadelphia to London and a return flight after the game resulted in stagnant blood flow to the injured leg. Inflammation from the injury along with dehydration from the game and jet lag all may have contributed to increased blood clotting.
Florida’s first-in-the-nation law
Beyond Hurts’ case, the most common risk factors to developing venous thromboembolism include hospitalization and surgery, especially orthopedic surgery and abdominal operations.

More than a third of cases occur following a hospital admission or just after discharge. Fractures and blunt trauma to the legs, prolonged immobility or bed rest, having a leg in a cast, or sitting for hours in a plane or car all predispose to blood clot formation in the legs. The use of estrogen in birth control pills or hormone therapy, cancer, pregnancy and inherited clotting disorders also predispose an otherwise healthy person to develop blood clots.

It is estimated that up to 70% of hospital-associated clots can be avoided with prophylactic blood thinners or inflatable leg devices called sequential compression devices to prevent deep vein thrombosis. However, fewer than half of hospital patients receive such measures, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

For people taking long trips in a car or plane, it is recommended to take frequent movement breaks, stay hydrated and even use compression socks. New symptoms of calf swelling, tenderness or redness should raise concerns for possible deep vein thrombosis.
Hurts had elite doctors and close monitoring, so his clots were caught and treated quickly. Most individuals do not have the same protections.

In 2025, Florida was the first state in the country to pass a law to help identify and treat those at risk of blood clots. It’s called the Emily Adkins Family Protection Act. Adkins tragically passed away in 2022 at age 23 from a fatal pulmonary embolism that occurred after a clot from her leg traveled to her lungs. Her family helped pass the bill that set up the nation’s first state blood clot and pulmonary embolism work group, which put forward the recommendations that later turned into law.

Florida’s law requires hospitals to have protocols to assess and treat patients at risk of blood clots and train hospital staff to recognize the symptoms of venous thromboembolism. It also will involve the creation of a statewide venous thromboembolism registry, the first of its kind in the country, where hospitals will report data on blood clots.

Florida is no longer alone. In 2026, the Blake Burgess Blood Clot Prevention Act was passed in Oklahoma; Mississippi proposed similar legislation. Advocates such as the National Blood Clot Alliance are urging other states to follow.

Hurts will most likely recover over the next few months. The outcome for many other individuals will depend on whether someone asks the right questions, recognizes the warning signs and acts in time. Venous thromboembolism is one of the few major killers where risk assessment, prevention, early diagnosis and fast treatment can play a critical role in changing the outcome.

articles.title: Why do people still get polio in some countries and not in others?
articles.author: Katrine L. Wallace, Assistant Professor of Epidemiology and Biostatistics, University of Illinois Chicago
paras: Curious Kids is a series for children of all ages. If you have a question you’d like an expert to answer, send it to CuriousKidsUS@theconversation.com.
Why are people still getting polio in some countries and in not others? – Mia, age 9, Centennial, Colorado

On a busy street in Karachi, Pakistan, a healthcare worker kneels down so she’s eye to eye with a toddler. She squeezes two drops of liquid onto the child’s tongue. Then she takes out a purple marker and colors the child’s pinkie fingernail so everyone can see that this toddler is now vaccinated against polio.
During big vaccination drives, thousands of health workers like her knock on doors across Pakistan.
Most kids in the United States will never experience anything like this, because they get the polio vaccine as a shot at the doctor’s office instead of drops in a door-to-door campaign.

The two vaccines work a little differently, but both protect kids from the polio virus. The countries that still see polio outbreaks are places where not enough people have gotten the preventive vaccine.

I’m an epidemiologist – a scientist who studies how diseases spread. My work focuses on diseases that vaccines can prevent, and on the false information that keeps some families from getting those vaccines.

Polio is caused by a virus that lives in the human gut. It spreads when tiny bits of poop from an infected person get onto hands, food or water, and then into someone else’s mouth. That’s why polio spreads fastest in places without clean water or good sewer systems.
Polio is sneaky. Most people who catch it never feel sick at all, so they can pass it on without knowing.
But in about 1 out of every 200 infections globally, the virus attacks the nerves that control muscles, usually in the legs. This can cause a person to be paralyzed for the rest of their life.
There is no cure for polio. But there is a vaccine, and a few doses can protect you for life.
How vaccines pushed polio back
In 1988, polio paralyzed about 350,000 children in 125 countries. That same year, countries around the world teamed up with one huge goal: Wipe out polio for good.
Though polio has not yet been entirely eliminated, this effort has been a major success. Since then, polio cases have dropped by more than 99% globally.
There used to be three types of wild polio virus. Now, only type 1 is left.
Where wild polio still hides
Wild polio, the original virus, now spreads in just two countries: Afghanistan and Pakistan. In 2025, wild polio paralyzed 52 children there.
Both countries have lived through decades of war. In some areas, it’s too dangerous for vaccinators to travel, and some have even been attacked.
In Afghanistan, vaccinators haven’t gone house to house since late 2024. Families must bring children to central spots, such as mosques, instead. But the kids who can’t get there miss their vaccines.
When too few kids are vaccinated
Some countries have outbreaks of a different kind, called vaccine-derived polio.

The oral polio vaccine, which is no longer used in many countries, including the U.S., contains a weakened polio virus – too weak to make a child sick, but strong enough to teach the body to fight polio.
After a child swallows the drops of vaccine, some of the weakened virus leaves their body in their poop. If nearly every kid around is vaccinated, the virus has nowhere to go and fizzles out.

But in areas where fewer than 80% of kids are vaccinated, it can pass from child to child. Like a message in a game of telephone, the virus changes a little each time it’s passed. Eventually, it can change back into a form that paralyzes children.
That might sound like the vaccine is the problem. But in fact, the problem is that too few kids have received the vaccine.

The children who go unvaccinated are usually the hardest to reach: kids in the poorest families, in faraway villages or in war zones. In one study in Pakistan, offering families other free healthcare along with polio drops cuts the share of never-vaccinated kids nearly in half.
The polio that went nowhere
In October 2025, scientists testing sewage in Hamburg, Germany, found wild polio. Its genes matched virus found in Afghanistan, more than 3,000 miles (4,800 kilometers) away.
This means that someone carrying the virus, probably without feeling sick, had traveled to Germany. But not a single child there was paralyzed because most German kids are vaccinated against polio.
Other countries in Europe found vaccine-derived polio in their sewage in 2025, with the same happy ending.
Polio can travel anywhere, but it can only hurt kids where they aren’t protected by the vaccine.

Polio also gets help spreading from rumors and misinformation. In 2003, false stories that the vaccine was harmful led parts of northern Nigeria to stop vaccinating for almost a year. This led to a small outbreak that spread from that area to other countries.
Research shows that false news online travels “farther, faster, deeper and more broadly than the truth.”

Unfortunately, misinformation could also contribute to a resurgence of polio in places where it has been eliminated – even the U.S. In Colorado, about 1 in 8 kindergartners haven’t had all their polio shots. And in 2022, vaccine-derived polio paralyzed an unvaccinated young man in New York.
Though rumors can travel quickly, trust is built one conversation at a time, by neighbors, religious leaders and doctors who take parents’ questions and concerns seriously.
So close to the finish line

Unfortunately, the budget of the worldwide program to end polio decreased by 30% in 2026, mostly because wealthy countries cut their foreign aid. This cut is largely led by the U.S., which withdrew from the World Health Organization, or WHO, officially in January 2026. Other wealthy donor governments like Germany and the U.K. have also made cuts.
The WHO has warned that these cuts mean that in some places, the fight against polio will not be able to continue.
Only one human disease has ever been wiped off the planet for good: smallpox, in 1980. Polio could be the second. The world has never been this close.
Somewhere today, a healthcare worker is coloring another tiny pinkie purple. Each one breaks a link in the chain that polio needs to survive.

articles.title: I composed music about infertility and pregnancy loss, then performed it in a Pittsburgh hospital
articles.author: Katherine Pukinskis, Assistant Professor of Music, Carnegie Mellon University
paras: It turns out you can rent a Steinway piano and have it delivered pretty much anywhere – including the lecture hall of a major working hospital.

In October 2025, I had one delivered to UPMC Magee-Womens Hospital in Pittsburgh for the premiere of “One in Four, One in Eight,” a 60-minute piece I composed about infertility and pregnancy loss, told through music, art, dance and narration.

Every October, families across the U.S. mark Pregnancy and Infant Loss Awareness Month, first proclaimed in 1988. This year, the observance arrives as federal funding cuts threaten reproductive health research, according to a report from the American Society for Reproductive Medicine. That matters because so much about why pregnancies end, or never begin, is still unknown.

“One in Four, One in Eight” is built around a piano quartet – piano, violin, viola and cello – with artwork and choreography woven in. The music creates a space to explore something deeply personal and physical that is often invisible from the outside and stigmatized. The project brings together the human and emotional sides of infertility and pregnancy loss with the procedural and scientific ones.
The piece takes its title from two statistics: 1 in 4 known pregnancies ends in loss in the U.S., and 1 in 8 women needs medical intervention to become and stay pregnant.

I am 1 in 4. I am 1 in 8. I’ve experienced the physical, emotional, social, financial, professional and psychological costs of infertility and pregnancy loss. As an assistant music professor and composer of contemporary classical music, I draw heavily on my own experiences as sources of inspiration; my creative practice is my research. But I also often consult external sources to inform aspects of my creative work.
Four movements, four stages

The piece has four movements, each tied to a stage or experience common in infertility or pregnancy loss. Before each one, a narrator lays out the scientific context of these deeply personal experiences.

The narrations drew on interviews with Dr. Gabriela Gosman, Dr. Pamela Parker, Dr. Allison Serra and physician assistant Carrie Weaver, all reproductive care providers at UPMC Magee-Womens Hospital. They also drew on research from the American Society for Reproductive Medicine, the National Institutes of Health, the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and the World Health Organization. Gosman reviewed and approved every narration for medical accuracy.

The first movement, “Antecedent,” is about anticipation and potential energy. Its narration presents pregnancy as a societal ideal, while noting that a live birth depends on a monthslong chain of events going just right. The music is bright and open-ended, invoking the best-case scenario. Even when it stalls, nothing is fully lost – listeners can still find a beat and tap along.

The second movement, “Fissure to Flow,” explores the friction between the body’s natural cycles and assisted reproductive technologies, or ART, which suppress and override those cycles. Pregnancy usually runs on its own clock, taking about 40 weeks from conception to birth. With ART, simply reaching a confirmed pregnancy can take months. Each round of in vitro fertilization, or IVF, is timed to a menstrual cycle, and doctors sometimes stop a round partway through, such as when the ovaries don’t respond as expected to medication. Up to 20% of rounds are stopped before eggs are ever retrieved, which means more waiting and starting over. Some people succeed after one round of IVF; others after several. Some never do.
Musically, in this movement, the four instruments playing gradually line up until they suddenly lock in, revealing how unsettled everything sounded before.
The third movement, “Somatic Drift,” is about loss and being lost. The music feels both aimless and intensely focused.
Pregnancy loss can stem from chromosomal or structural abnormalities, such as a uterine septum, fibroids or scar tissue. It can also stem from hormone imbalances involving prolactin or progesterone.
Yet about half of all pregnancy losses are unexplained. That’s not because there is no cause, but limited research and funding leave doctors with few tools to find one.

The final movement, “Fortified,” is about the calm that comes with information, though this doesn’t make it a happy ending. Its grounded music acknowledges the financial, physical, emotional and professional costs of infertility and pregnancy loss. The narration highlights changes in care I hope to see, from better pain management for invasive procedures to in-office childcare for last-minute appointments, along with new research and legislation to support ART.

To be fortified is to be made stronger. Bodies hold on to pregnancy, too. Cells from a pregnancy can remain in a person’s body for years afterward, whether the pregnancy lasted four days or 40 weeks. This is a phenomenon called fetal microchimerism.

“One in Four, One in Eight” was designed to reach beyond a typical concert audience. Alongside the music and the narrated science, the performances featured the San Antonio-based chamber ensemble Agarita Chamber Players, who performed the piece, along with choreography by Pittsburgh-based Attack Theatre and new visual art works by Pittsburgh visual artist Morgan Overton. Both Attack Theatre and Overton created their work in response to the music, and it debuted live during the performances.

To make the concerts easier to attend, tickets and on-site childcare were free, and the project paid for parking. Before each concert, the project team hosted talks with me and the other artists to welcome people into the conversation. Afterward, receptions gave nonprofit community organizations space to share information and resources.

The science and music in “One in Four, One in Eight” depend on one another. Where a clinical setting is a crucial component of health and healing, public performances create spaces for learning, understanding and catharsis.

articles.title: AI chatbots can be a valuable health resource for older adults – if they embrace ‘informed skepticism’
articles.author: Robin Brewer, Associate Professor of Information, University of Michigan
paras: It’s easy to stereotype older adults as tech-averse or novice tech users. Yet a growing number of adults age 60 and older are embracing artificial intelligence, using it for entertainment, planning trips and even accessing health information.

I study how people interact with computers and technology – and specifically, how older adults use voice assistants and AI-powered chatbots like Amazon Alexa and ChatGPT to engage with information. Using AI for health information can be particularly fraught because chatbots can be so helpful in explaining complex medical information, but also risky if users automatically trust the responses they receive.

My research suggests that the most productive way of engaging with health information generated by an AI chatbot is from a position of informed skepticism – that is, remaining open-minded, yet using built-in features to evaluate the credibility and quality of chatbot responses.

About 1 in 5 adults turn to AI chatbots to ask questions about health, according to a 2025 survey of 300 adults. Questions might include asking about symptoms or seeking advice about diet and fitness. The chatbots might be mainstream services such as Claude, Gemini, ChatGPT or systems designed for a specific health provider.

People turn to these tools for many reasons. It can be easier to talk to a chatbot about sensitive topics, and chatbots reply almost instantaneously – much quicker than making an appointment to see your doctor weeks or months down the line. Chatbots can also explain complex topics in new ways and condense an overwhelming amount of information into a simple summary.

Although older people may be less likely than others to use AI, I’ve found in my own work that older people often use voice assistants like Siri and Alexa to ask health questions. Similarly, a poll I conducted with colleagues in 2025 shows that 1 in 2 older adults report using AI chatbots or voice assistants, and about 14% of people in this group are accessing health information.

Older adults often experience more health needs than younger adults due to long-term chronic health conditions or new age-related diagnoses. More health needs often means more health-related questions.

AI is particularly appealing for health questions because people get answers faster than searching across multiple websites when using a search engine – or having to wait for a healthcare visit. Moreover, being able to use chatbots and voice assistants at home can make people feel more in control of their health, compared with clinical settings where older people’s autonomy can be overlooked or where they may experience being excluded in lieu of conversations with caregivers.
Although older people may use chatbots to supplement or replace medical professionals, AI use has risks.

For example, it can provide incorrect advice in medical emergencies, misclassify health conditions and be overly agreeable, responding with what it deduces the user wants to hear, even if the response is not factually accurate. AI experts call this last tendency “sycophancy.”

But these inaccuracies can be hard for a user to detect. AI-powered chatbots draw on vast amounts of data and use pattern-matching to predict words most likely to come next in a sentence. That means the output can appear correct but contain inaccurate information.

Most mainstream chatbots include a warning under the dialogue box noting that their output might contain mistakes, but it is often in small or gray text, making it easy to overlook. The warning is meant to encourage cross-checking information with published sources, but users rarely do so. In the 2025 survey mentioned above of 300 adults who used a health chatbot, 4 in 5 admitted they never verified its output.

In my own research, I found that older people searching with a voice assistant preferred to begin and complete their search process on the same device, suggesting they are unlikely to verify an AI chatbot’s output if it takes them to a different format. In contrast, younger adults expected AI to be a step in the search process, guiding them to seeking further information with the help of another option, such as a search engine. This difference makes it critical to provide strategies to older people as they use AI.

Another risk is privacy, since AI companies that make public chatbots often keep user prompts for training future models. Researchers generally recommend that users not include personally identifiable information when asking questions to chatbots.
Strategies for safer searching

Awareness that older adults may use AI in ways distinct from other demographic groups – and may encounter specific challenges – is growing. A bipartisan bill, the Aging with AI Act, introduced in the U.S. Senate in 2026, for example, underscores the need for more research on both its benefits and its risks.
My research points to a few guidelines to start with:

Learn how to opt out of AI. Although mainstream chatbots like ChatGPT are popular, the most common way people access AI is through a search engine because AI features are often built directly into search results. Some search engines, like Microsoft’s Bing, ask people to opt into using AI. Others, like Google Search, rely on users to opt out of AI.

Google shares an AI-generated summary at the top of each search result. To opt out when searching for information using Google, adding “-ai” to the end of the search query will remove AI content. Opting out of AI might be useful when searching for particularly sensitive health information that you wish to keep private.

Use the information quality features. Most AI chatbots have features that allow users to confirm the source of its output. For example, Claude, Gemini and ChatGPT include links to sources they used to predict the response. Make sure you explore these sources to confirm they are legitimate and to get more details that can help you find the information you need.

Further, you can change the model the chatbot is using, which can change how much depth the chatbot goes into in its response. For example, Gemini has a drop-down menu next to the search box that includes “flash-lite,” “flash” and “pro” models. Chatbots’ more advanced versions provide more thorough responses that can help users better determine information quality.
And users can report inaccurate, toxic or harmful content by clicking the thumbs down icon shown at the bottom of the response.

Ask better questions. Ask for objective information that can be verified, rather than subjective advice, particularly in high-risk health contexts. For example, instead of asking “which high blood pressure medicine should I take?” ask “what are the side effects of” a particular high blood pressure medicine.

And to prevent sycophancy, phrase questions neutrally. For example, instead of asking “Is it a good idea to get a flu shot?” a searcher can instead type “Tell me about the pros and cons of getting flu shots.”

Don’t use AI as a replacement for medical professionals. Health-related chatbot output is best used collaboratively with a medical professional. This might include saving the chatbot output to discuss during your next healthcare appointment, using chatbots to understand complex diagnoses from your doctor, or getting a chatbot to suggest questions to ask your doctor during your next visit.

Most importantly, confirm health-related answers that result in making changes to your health routine with your healthcare provider. A knowledgeable, licensed healthcare provider is best qualified to determine how general information about illness or treatments would apply to your specific situation.

articles.title: How the body clock could help personalise depression treatment
articles.author: Timothy Hearn, Lecturer, University of Cambridge; Anglia Ruskin University
paras: A person with depression might sleep much longer than usual and still wake feeling exhausted. Later that evening, when they want to go to bed, they may find themselves wide awake. Researchers are investigating whether patterns like these could help explain why antidepressants work better for some people than others.
The clue may lie in the body’s internal clock, which helps regulate when someone sleeps, wakes and feels alert.

An Australian study examined 11,380 people, predominantly with severe or recurring depression. About 23% met the researchers’ criteria for a proposed subtype called “circadian depression”, named after the body’s roughly 24-hour internal clock.

Participants needed at least three of six features, including being a night owl, sleeping longer during depression, morning tiredness and seasonal changes in mood or behaviour. The other features involved habitually sleeping and waking later, and having different sleep schedules on working days and days off.

Compared with other participants, this group reported less benefit and more side-effects from two common types of antidepressants, SSRIs and SNRIs, which affect how brain cells communicate through chemical messengers. However, some people with these sleep patterns still reported benefiting from these medicines.

The researchers also found genetic associations with later sleep timing, reduced sensitivity to insulin, the hormone that helps regulate blood sugar, and a protein involved in inflammation, the immune system’s response to injury or infection. These associations reflect inherited tendencies, rather than evidence that participants actually had blood-sugar problems or inflammation.

The findings are preliminary. Participants recalled their symptoms and medication experiences, and those in the proposed group generally had more severe depression. The researchers did not measure their internal clocks or establish cause and effect.

Some features overlap with recognised forms of depression, so it remains unclear whether this is a distinct subtype. All participants had European genetic ancestry, limiting how widely the findings can be applied. The 23% figure therefore cannot be assumed to represent everyone with depression.
How the body clock affects mood

The body clock coordinates roughly 24-hour cycles, known as circadian rhythms, which affect sleepiness, body temperature and hormones, the chemical messengers that help regulate the body. Light reaching the eyes helps keep this clock aligned with day and night. Meals and physical activity also provide timing cues.

When internal timing clashes with daily demands, sleep can suffer. Someone whose clock runs late may feel alert at midnight but have to get up for work while their body is still expecting sleep. Being a night owl is not necessarily a problem. Persistent disruption is the concern.
Sleep and mental health can reinforce one another. Disrupted sleep may worsen depression, while depression and stress can disturb sleep and daily routines.

One possible link involves brain systems that regulate emotion and reward, including the ability to enjoy pleasurable experiences. Animal experiments suggest that disrupting the body clock can affect these systems and produce depression-like behaviour.

In small laboratory experiments, researchers altered the sleep schedules of shift workers and people who did not work shifts. When their sleep and waking times were out of step with their internal clocks, participants reported worse mood. They had not been recruited because they had depression, and temporary low mood is different from clinical depression.

Conventional antidepressants might leave a timing problem untreated, but that remains a hypothesis. The Australian study did not test body-clock treatments, and its findings cannot establish whether someone with disrupted rhythms would benefit more from an alternative medication.

Light therapy involves sitting near a specially designed bright-light box at a scheduled time, often in the morning. Morning light can shift a late-running body clock earlier, helping someone feel sleepy and wake earlier.

The treatment is used for seasonal affective disorder, depression that follows a seasonal pattern, often during darker months. Evidence suggests it can also help with depression that has no seasonal pattern.

A review of 11 clinical trials involving 858 people examined bright-light therapy for non-seasonal depression, including bipolar depression. Bipolar disorder involves depression alongside episodes of unusually elevated or irritable mood and increased energy.

In trials reporting remission, about 41% of people receiving bright light improved enough to fall below the threshold for depression, compared with 24% receiving dim light or treatment without bright light.

But these trials did not select people with the proposed circadian subtype, so they cannot tell us whether that group benefits more. Light may also influence mood through brain pathways separate from the body clock.

Timing and medical guidance matter. Light can shift the clock earlier or later depending on when it is used. People with bipolar disorder need particular supervision because light therapy can sometimes trigger unusually elevated or irritable mood.

Regular waking times, daytime activity and meals may also support daily rhythms. Melatonin, a hormone that rises in the evening and signals biological night, can help shift a delayed clock when carefully timed. However, studies have not established melatonin supplements as an effective depression treatment.
Towards more personalised treatment

Could measuring someone’s internal clock help doctors choose treatments? Wrist-worn activity monitors can estimate sleep patterns, while saliva samples taken throughout an evening can show when melatonin starts rising, offering a more direct measure of internal timing.
Researchers need to establish whether the proposed group really has distinct biological rhythms, then test whether choosing treatment based on those measurements helps people recover sooner.
For now, sleep patterns cannot reliably predict which antidepressant will work best, and the findings provide no reason to change prescribed medication without medical advice.
If future trials confirm a benefit, a prescription for depression might one day specify when to receive light as carefully as which medicine to take.

articles.title: Long COVID linked to greater risk of high blood pressure
articles.author: Pia Lindberg, RN, PhD, Department of Medicine, Karolinska Institutet
paras: Long COVID is often associated with symptoms such as persistent fatigue, shortness of breath and brain fog. But evidence increasingly shows that long COVID may have a broad effect on the cardiovascular system, as well.

Previously, our research found that long COVID was associated with higher risk of heart disease. Now, our latest study shows that people who have long COVID are at greater risk of developing hypertension (high blood pressure). This risk was found even in people whose initial COVID infection was mild and did not require hospitalisation.

Our study included more than 1.2 million Swedish adults aged 18 to 65 living in Stockholm County. We used data from the MIRACLE-S cohort, which tracks diagnoses, healthcare visits, hospitalisations and prescription information from these participants.

Participants with pre-existing hypertension and those hospitalised with COVID were excluded from our analysis. This allowed us to focus on milder infections and the long-term effects COVID may have on blood pressure.
Between October 2020 and January 2025, 8,365 (0.7%) participants were diagnosed with long COVID. During follow-up, 18% of all participants were diagnosed with hypertension.

Overall, the incidence of hypertension in the long COVID group was between 22% and 23% during the follow-up period. After adjusting for other factors that may affect hypertension risk – such as age, socioeconomic status and whether a person was diagnosed with any other health conditions – this meant that people with long COVID had a 14% higher risk of hypertension than those who did not have long COVID.
When analysed by sex, the risk of hypertension was similar in women and men. But among those with long COVID, hypertension occurred in 16% of women and 24% of men.

We also found that the association between long COVID and hypertension was stronger in older age groups. This makes sense, given age is associated with many changes to cardiovascular health that can increase blood pressure. For instance, the arteries tend to become stiffer in old age. This forces the heart to work harder in order to pump blood.

The association between long COVID and hypertension was also stronger in people who were diagnosed with diabetes. This may indicate that all three conditions share overlapping cardiometabolic mechanisms. These findings will need to be confirmed in future research.
Long COVID and hypertension
There are several interconnected mechanisms that may explain the association we observed between long COVID and hypertension.

For instance, studies have shown that in healthy adults, a COVID infection can impair arterial function and alter blood pressure for up to three years. Such physiological changes may help to explain the link that our study showed between long COVID and hypertension.

But as our research was an observational study, it meant we couldn’t directly measure factors such as blood pressure or arterial stiffness. This means future research will need to investigate whether such cardiometabolic changes can explain the link between hypertension and long COVID.

Our study also did not collect information on treatments that may have been initiated during follow-up which might have affected blood pressure. It will be important for future studies to better adjust for these factors so that we can better understand the connection between long COVID and hypertension.

Still, our findings may have important implications for clinical practice. Hypertension remains one of the key factors that can be changed to reduce the risk of cardiovascular disease, such as coronary heart disease. Understanding that people who have long COVID are at increased risk of experiencing hypertension could provide an important opportunity to intervene early and prevent cardiovascular disease.

The findings also suggest that people with long COVID should have blood pressure assessments performed more frequently – particularly if they have additional cardiovascular risk factors. But whether a specific enhanced screening strategy improves outcomes remains to be established.

As our understanding of COVID evolves, it’s becoming increasingly apparent that the virus’s impact on health can persist long after the initial infection. This could have implications not only for cardiovascular health, but for the management of many chronic diseases.
